title: The Foucault Century
author: Michael C. Behrent
content:
![The Foucault
Century](https://storage.ghost.io/c/65/af/65afbdb5-30bf-4286-acc4-9535069adb42/content/images/2026/10/Screenshot-2026-10-14-at-11.39.37
---PM-2-1.png)

Michel Foucault, by some counts the world's most cited author, was born a
hundred years ago today. Though he died forty-two years ago, the controversial
philosopher's image remains remarkably cutting-edge. Foucault's signature
concepts--power/knowledge, panopticism, biopower--still sound deliciously
subversive. Though he died too soon to be drawn into our never-ending culture
wars, he continues to be associated--negatively or positively--with queer
theory, the critique of the gender binary, prison abolition, and
postcolonialism.

Yet if one visits Foucault's granite tombstone in a gray, drab cemetery along
a country road in the Poitou region of France, it is hard not to see him from
a different perspective. He seems _old_. As he turns one hundred, could it be
that Foucault stands out less for his ongoing relevance than as a throwback to
a world we have lost?

Ever since he burst onto the intellectual scene in France in the 1960s, then
crossed the Atlantic to become a leading figure of "French Theory" or
"postmodernism" in the United States in the 1970s and '80s, Foucault
challenged conventional wisdom and proposed giddily new ways of thinking. His
work on the historical conditions of knowledge, the dissemination of
"micropowers," and the social function of "normality" seemed to overtake and
then lap the twentieth century's most radical forms of thought. Foucault
appeared to out-Marx Marx, psychoanalyze Freud, and achieve a deeper level of
authenticity than existentialism. He was fond of slogans that showcased his
readiness to dispense with the past. He predicted the "death of the author,"
described "man" as a recent "invention" that was "nearing its end," and
dismissed the state as a concept that was useless to political analysis. He
described a book by Jean-Paul Sartre--the defining French intellectual of the
postwar era--as a failed "attempt by a nineteenth-century man to understand
the twentieth century."

The sense of Foucault's prescience continues to shape how he is seen today. In
July, a _New York Times_ essay declared: "[_From AI to the Deep State, Michel
Foucault Foresaw It
All_](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/07/10/books/review/michel-foucault-ai-tech-
power.html?ref=compactmag.com)." Many conservatives find fault precisely with
Foucault's radical modernity, as do some left-of-center critics of wokeness,
such as [_Susan
Nieman_](https://www.politybooks.com/bookdetail?book_slug=left-is-not-woke--
9781509558308&ref=compactmag.com) and [_Yascha
Mounk_](https://www.penguinrandomhouse.com/books/712961/the-identity-trap-by-
yascha-mounk/?ref=compactmag.com).

> "Consider the world in which he lived."

Foucault's birth centenary may be the moment to ask whether his avant-garde
reputation is exaggerated. Consider the world in which he lived. Foucault was
born to a bourgeois family in the regional capital of Poitiers, where his
father and grandfather were both prominent doctors. He remained in this milieu
until, at the age of eighteen, he moved to Paris to study in 1945. Foucault's
concerns were [_decisively
shaped_](https://www.pennpress.org/9781512825145/becoming-
foucault/?ref=compactmag.com) by the provincial world in which he was raised.
